advances: Refutes the proposed dimension-independent bound on parity-conditioned off-diagonal probability in terms of parity imbalance and midpoint total variation. The counterexamples have globally log-concave extensions agreeing at every lattice zero, and their Hellinger gains tend to infinity. Thus this is an obstruction to that particular quantitative rigidity bridge, not a disproof of small-gain heavy-atom stability or the weak Oertel conjecture.

proof:
We first construct and estimate the seed for every integer \(L\ge2\). This also permits a small exact census at the end. Set \(R=1+2^L\), and write the coordinates of \(\mathbb R^\nu\) as \(z=(x,(y_{i,h})_{1\le i\le L,\,1\le h\le m_i})\). Indeed, \(1+\sum_{i=1}^Lm_i=1+L(2^L-2)=\nu\). Let \(\mathcal P\) be the polytope defined by \(0\le x\le R\) and, for all \(i,h\),

\[
-\frac{(R-1)x}{R2^i}\le y_{i,h}\le1,
\qquad
y_{i,h}\le1-\frac{x-1}{2^i}.
\]

All coefficients are rational, the coordinate bounds make \(\mathcal P\) compact, and \([0,1]^\nu\subseteq\mathcal P\), so it is full-dimensional. Define \(w_z=t^{(x-1)_+}\mathbf1_{\mathcal P}(z)\) on \(\mathbb Z^\nu\), where \((x-1)_+=\max\{x-1,0\}\), and put \(W=\sum_z w_z\), \(p_z=w_z/W\). The support is finite and nonempty. The function

\[
f(z)=\frac1W\exp\bigl(-L(\log2)(x-1)_+\bigr)\mathbf1_{\mathcal P}(z),
\qquad z\in\mathbb R^\nu,
\]

is finite-valued and agrees with \(p\) at every lattice point. If both endpoints lie in \(\mathcal P\), convexity keeps their segment in \(\mathcal P\), and convexity of \((x-1)_+\) gives the log-concavity inequality for the exponential factor. If an endpoint lies outside \(\mathcal P\), the required right-hand side is zero. This proves global log-concavity, including all zero lattice values.

We enumerate every lattice point of \(\mathcal P\). At \(x=0\), each transverse coordinate has exactly the integer choices \(0,1\). At \(x=1\), its lower bound lies strictly between \(-1\) and \(0\), and its upper bound is \(1\), giving the same choices. These two fibers are the core \(\mathcal C=\{0,1\}^\nu\). Every core point has weight \(1\), and there is exactly one core point of each parity class.

The remaining possible integer heights are \(x=r+1\), with \(1\le r\le2^L\). Set \(\beta=1-(r+1)/R\), so \(0\le\beta<1\). At this height a coordinate in block \(i\) lies in the interval \([-(r+\beta)/2^i,\,1-r/2^i]\). To find its integers, write \(r=a2^i+s\), \(0\le s<2^i\). If \(s=0\), its ceiling lower endpoint is \(-a\) and its upper endpoint is \(1-a\). If \(s>0\), then \(0<s+\beta<2^i\), so its ceiling lower endpoint and floor upper endpoint are both \(-a\). Thus the complete set of choices is

\[
I_i(r)=
\begin{cases}
\{-r/2^i,\,1-r/2^i\},&2^i\mid r,\\
\{-\lfloor r/2^i\rfloor\},&2^i\nmid r.
\end{cases}
\]

The coordinates are independently constrained once the height is fixed, so these intervals enumerate the full support. If \(r=(2\ell+1)2^k\), where \(0\le k\le L\), that fiber has \(2^{\sum_{i=1}^km_i}=2^{L(2^k-1)-k}\) points, each of weight \(t^r\). The exponent is zero when \(k=0\).

Call the fibers with \(r=2^k\), \(0\le k\le L\), the peak fibers, and denote their lattice sets by \(\mathcal A_k\). Their masses are

\[
A_k:=\sum_{z\in\mathcal A_k}w_z
=2^{L(2^k-1)-k}t^{2^k}
=\frac{t}{2^k}.
\]

Let \(F\) be the total mass of the other tail fibers and \(T\) the mass of all points outside \(\mathcal C\). For fixed valuation \(k\), the nonpeak heights have \(\ell\ge1\), and their fiber masses equal \((t/2^k)t^{2\ell2^k}\). Extending their finite sums to geometric series gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
F&\le\sum_{k=0}^{L-1}\frac{t}{2^k}
          \sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty}t^{2\ell2^k}\\
&\le\frac{t^2}{1-t^2}\sum_{k=0}^{L-1}\frac{t}{2^k}
\le\frac{2t^3}{1-t^2}\le3t^3.
\end{aligned}
\]

Here \(t\le1/4\) and \(t^{2\ell2^k}\le t^{2\ell}\) justify the second line. Since \(\sum_{k=0}^LA_k=2t-t^2\), we have \(t\le T\le3t\), \(W=2^\nu+T\), and \(A_L=t^2\).

For a tail point \(z\), let \(b(z)\in\mathcal C\) be its unique same-parity core point, and put \(\sigma(z)=(z+b(z))/2\). On each integer coordinate this map is exactly the ceiling of half that coordinate. We claim that \(\sigma:\mathcal A_k\to\mathcal A_{k-1}\) is exactly \(2^{m_k}\)-to-one for every \(1\le k\le L\). Its height map is \(1+2^k\mapsto1+2^{k-1}\). In block \(i<k\), the two source choices are \(-2^{k-i}\) and \(1-2^{k-i}\). Their images are respectively \(-2^{k-i-1}\) and \(1-2^{k-i-1}\), the two distinct choices in \(\mathcal A_{k-1}\). In block \(k\), the source choices \(-1,0\) both map to \(0\); this gives two choices independently in each of its \(m_k\) coordinates. All blocks \(i>k\) are zero in both fibers. This proves both surjectivity and the exact multiplicity.

Consequently, at every \(j\in\mathcal A_{k-1}\), the ordered same-parity core-tail pairs whose tail endpoint lies in \(\mathcal A_k\) have total weight

\[
2\cdot2^{m_k}t^{2^k}
=2^{L2^{k-1}}t^{2^k}
=t^{2^{k-1}}=w_j.
\]

The factor \(2\) accounts for the two endpoint orders. The first peak \(\mathcal A_0\) is the single point \((2,\mathbf0)\), of weight \(t\). Its core partner is \((0,\mathbf0)\), and their midpoint is \(c=(1,\mathbf0)\); these two ordered pairs contribute \(2t\) at \(c\).

For each parity class \(b\), set \(\tau_b=\sum_{z\notin\mathcal C,\,z\equiv b\pmod2}w_z\) and \(B=\sum_b\tau_b^2\). Then \(\sum_b\tau_b=T\), \(0\le B\le T^2\le9t^2\). Each parity class has unnormalized mass \(1+\tau_b\), so the total unnormalized same-parity ordered-pair mass is \(D=\sum_b(1+\tau_b)^2=2^\nu+2T+B\), and \(q=D/W^2\). Therefore

\[
2^\nu q-1
=\frac{2^\nu B-T^2}{(2^\nu+T)^2}
\le\frac{B}{2^\nu}
\le\frac{9t^2}{2^\nu}.
\]

The numerator is nonnegative by Cauchy-Schwarz applied to the \(2^\nu\) numbers \(\tau_b\). It is strictly positive here. Indeed, \(\tau_0\ge t\) because \((2,\mathbf0)\) is in the tail. On the other hand, consider a parity class with even height and two different parity bits in two coordinates of block \(L\). This is possible because \(m_L\ge3\). Every even-height tail point has odd \(r\), hence \(r<2^L\), and all its block-\(L\) coordinates are zero by the interval formula. Thus this parity class has tail mass zero. The \(\tau_b\) are not constant, proving strict positivity.

Within each parity class, expanding the square of its tail mass gives \(B\ge\sum_{z\notin\mathcal C}w_z^2\). It follows that the conditional off-diagonal probability \(a(p):=\Gamma\{X\ne Y\}\) satisfies

\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p)&=1-\frac{2^\nu+\sum_{z\notin\mathcal C}w_z^2}{D}\\
&=\frac{2T+B-\sum_{z\notin\mathcal C}w_z^2}{D}
\ge\frac{2T}{D}.
\end{aligned}
\]

As \(L\ge2\), we have \(2^\nu\ge32\), and \(6t+9t^2\le33/16\le2^\nu\). Hence \(D\le2^\nu+6t+9t^2\le2\cdot2^\nu\), and \(a(p)\ge t/2^\nu\).

We next prove the squared Hellinger estimate. Define the unnormalized midpoint table \(\mathcal R_j=\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z^\nu}w_{j+v}w_{j-v}\). The map \((j,v)\mapsto(j+v,j-v)\) is a bijection between integer center-displacement pairs and ordered same-parity lattice endpoint pairs. Thus \(\sum_j\mathcal R_j=D\), and \(p^{\mathrm{mid}}_j=\mathcal R_j/D\). In normalized notation, \(\mathcal R_j/W^2=\sum_vp_{j+v}p_{j-v}\).

Consider the nonnegative reference table

\[
U_j=\mathbf1_{\mathcal C}(j)
    +2t\mathbf1_{\{c\}}(j)
    +w_j\mathbf1_{\bigcup_{k=0}^{L-1}\mathcal A_k}(j).
\]

The first term comprises all same-parity core-core pairs, which are precisely the diagonal core pairs. The remaining terms comprise all ordered core-tail pairs whose tail endpoint lies in a peak, by the exact multiplicity calculation. The unaccounted pairs are all ordered core-tail pairs with nonpeak tail endpoint, of total mass \(2F\), and all same-parity tail-tail pairs, of total mass \(B\). Therefore \(\mathcal R_j\ge U_j\) for every \(j\), and \(\sum_j(\mathcal R_j-U_j)=2F+B\). These identities account for every pair, including overlaps between their possible midpoint locations.

For finite nonnegative tables define \(\mathcal E(u,v)=\sum_j(\sqrt{u_j}-\sqrt{v_j})^2\). The tables \(w\) and \(U\) agree except at \(c\), the last peak, and the nonpeak tail. The inequalities \((\sqrt{1+2t}-1)^2=4t^2/(\sqrt{1+2t}+1)^2\le t^2\) and \((\sqrt{u+e}-\sqrt u)^2\le e\) for \(u,e\ge0\) yield

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal E(w,U)&=(\sqrt{1+2t}-1)^2+A_L+F
                  \le t^2+A_L+F,\\
\mathcal E(U,\mathcal R)&\le2F+B,\\
\mathcal E(w,\mathcal R)&\le
             2\mathcal E(w,U)+2\mathcal E(U,\mathcal R)
             \le2t^2+2A_L+6F+2B.
\end{aligned}
\]

The third line follows by writing each difference of square roots as the sum through \(\sqrt{U_j}\) and using \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\). All tables have finite support.

Normalization is handled by an exact identity rather than an estimate on the separate masses:

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{\mathrm H}^2(p,p^{\mathrm{mid}})
&=1-\frac{\sum_j\sqrt{w_j\mathcal R_j}}{\sqrt{WD}}\\
&=\frac{\mathcal E(w,\mathcal R)-(\sqrt W-\sqrt D)^2}
        {2\sqrt{WD}}\\
&\le\frac{t^2+A_L+3F+B}{2^\nu}
\le\frac{11t^2+9t^3}{2^\nu}
\le\frac{14t^2}{2^\nu}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Here \(W,D\ge2^\nu\), \(A_L=t^2\), \(F\le3t^3\), \(B\le9t^2\), and \(t\le1/4\) were used. This proves all three seed bounds.

Now let \(L\ge4\), and take the integer \(N=2^\nu/t\). Define \(P_L=p^{\otimes N}\) on \(\mathbb Z^{n_L}\), where \(n_L=N\nu\). Its extension is the product \(f_L(z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(N)})=\prod_{\ell=1}^N f(z^{(\ell)})\). This function is finite-valued, has convex compact support \(\mathcal P^N\), and agrees with every lattice value, including zeros. Multiplying the individual log-concavity inequalities proves its global log-concavity.

Before conditioning, the \(N\) endpoint pairs are independent with law \(p\otimes p\). Equal parity of the full vectors is the intersection of the \(N\) blockwise equal-parity events, each of probability \(q>0\). The conditional probability of any tuple of block endpoint pairs therefore factors as the product of the \(N\) corresponding seed conditional probabilities. This gives

\[
q_L=q^N,\qquad
P_L^{\mathrm{mid}}=(p^{\mathrm{mid}})^{\otimes N},\qquad
\Gamma_L\{X=Y\}=(1-a(p))^N.
\]

Using \(1-u\le e^{-u}\) for \(0\le u\le1\), we obtain \(\Gamma_L\{X\ne Y\}\ge1-e^{-Na(p)}\ge1-e^{-1}\). The parity estimate gives

\[
0<2^{n_L}q_L-1
=(2^\nu q)^N-1
\le\left(1+\frac{9t^2}{2^\nu}\right)^N-1
\le e^{9t}-1.
\]

For probability tables \(u,v\), their Hellinger affinity \(\sum_j\sqrt{u_jv_j}=1-d_{\mathrm H}^2(u,v)\) multiplies under products, by expanding the finite sums. Thus

\[
d_{\mathrm H}^2(P_L,P_L^{\mathrm{mid}})
=1-\left(1-d_{\mathrm H}^2(p,p^{\mathrm{mid}})\right)^N
\le N d_{\mathrm H}^2(p,p^{\mathrm{mid}})
\le14t.
\]

The middle inequality follows from \(1-(1-u)^N\le Nu\), \(0\le u\le1\). Cauchy-Schwarz also gives the elementary comparison

\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{TV}(u,v)
&=\frac12\sum_j|\sqrt{u_j}-\sqrt{v_j}|(\sqrt{u_j}+\sqrt{v_j})\\
&\le\frac12\sqrt{2d_{\mathrm H}^2(u,v)}
       \sqrt{\sum_j(\sqrt{u_j}+\sqrt{v_j})^2}
\le\sqrt{2d_{\mathrm H}^2(u,v)},
\end{aligned}
\]

because the last sum is \(2+2\sum_j\sqrt{u_jv_j}\le4\). Consequently \(\operatorname{TV}(P_L^{\mathrm{mid}},P_L)\le\sqrt{28t}\). For \(0\le u\le1\), convexity of the exponential gives \(e^u-1\le(e-1)u\le2u\); the bound \(e<3\) also follows immediately from its power series. Since \(9t\le9/16<1\),

\[
\sqrt{2^{n_L}q_L-1}+\operatorname{TV}(P_L^{\mathrm{mid}},P_L)
\le\sqrt{18t}+\sqrt{28t}<10\sqrt t.
\]

Indeed, \((\sqrt{18}+\sqrt{28})^2=46+2\sqrt{504}<100\). The denominator is positive by the strict parity inequality. Since \(e>2\), the numerator is greater than \(1/2\), proving the stated ratio bound and the failure of every finite universal \(C\).

Finally, we verify the gain assertion directly. For the unnormalized seed write \(H_j(w)=\sum_v\sqrt{w_{j+v}w_{j-v}}\), so \(H_j(p)=H_j(w)/W\). At \(c=(1,\mathbf0)\), the zero displacement contributes \(1\), and the two oriented displacements joining \((0,\mathbf0)\) and \((2,\mathbf0)\) contribute \(2\sqrt t\). Hence

\[
e^{G(p)}
=\frac{2^\nu H_*(w)}{W}
\ge\frac{2^\nu(1+2\sqrt t)}{2^\nu+T}
\ge1+\sqrt t.
\]

For the last inequality it suffices that \(T(1+\sqrt t)\le2^\nu\sqrt t\). This follows from \(T\le3t\), \(3\sqrt t(1+\sqrt t)\le9/4\), and \(2^\nu\ge32\). Expanding the displacement sums for a product table gives \(H_{(j_1,\ldots,j_N)}(P_L)=\prod_{\ell=1}^N H_{j_\ell}(p)\). Every factor has an attained finite maximum, since the seed is finitely supported. Choosing its maximizing center in each block shows \(H_*(P_L)=H_*(p)^N\), and therefore \(G(P_L)=NG(p)\). The bound \(\log(1+u)=\int_0^u(1+s)^{-1}\,ds\ge u/2\) for \(0\le u\le1\) now gives \(G(P_L)\ge N\sqrt t/2=2^\nu/(2\sqrt t)\to\infty\). These examples consequently do not approach the small-gain regime.

For an independent exact check of the support and pair counts, specialize the seed to \(L=2\). Then \(t=1/4\), \(\nu=5\), \(m_1=1\), and \(m_2=3\). The core has \(32\) points. The four tail heights \(x=2,3,4,5\) have respectively \(1,2,1,16\) points, each of respective weight \(1/4,1/16,1/64,1/256\). Thus there are \(52\) supported points, \(F=1/64\), \(T=29/64\), and \(W=2077/64\). At even height the two tail parity classes have masses \(1/4\) and \(1/64\). At odd height the last peak contributes \(1/256\) to each of its \(16\) parity classes, and the second peak adds \(1/16\) to two of those classes. Their tail parity masses are therefore \(17/256\) twice and \(1/256\) fourteen times. Direct squaring gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
B&=(1/4)^2+(1/64)^2+2(17/256)^2+14(1/256)^2
   =147/2048,\\
\sum_{z\notin\mathcal C}w_z^2
&=(1/4)^2+2(1/16)^2+(1/64)^2+16(1/256)^2
   =145/2048,\\
D&=32+2(29/64)+147/2048=67539/2048,\\
a(p)&=1858/67539,\qquad
2^\nu q-1=8567/4313929.
\end{aligned}
\]

Here the peak midpoint multiplicities are \(2^{m_1}=2\) and \(2^{m_2}=8\), giving the exact balances \(2\cdot2\cdot(1/16)=1/4\) and \(2\cdot8\cdot(1/256)=1/16\). This census follows directly from the displayed intervals and rational arithmetic; the proof for arbitrary \(L\) does not rely on a computational enumeration.
statement:
For a finitely supported probability table \(p\) on \(\mathbb Z^n\), define \(\pi_b=\sum_{z\equiv b\pmod2}p_z\), \(q=\sum_{b\in(\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z)^n}\pi_b^2\), and let \(\Gamma\) be the law of independent \(X,Y\) with law \(p\), conditioned on \(X\equiv Y\pmod2\). Let \(p^{\mathrm{mid}}\) be the law of \((X+Y)/2\) under \(\Gamma\), and use \(\operatorname{TV}(u,v)=\frac12\sum_z|u_z-v_z|\). Define \(H_j(p)=\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z^n}\sqrt{p_{j+v}p_{j-v}}\), \(H_*(p)=\max_jH_j(p)\), and \(G(p)=\log(2^nH_*(p))\), with natural logarithms and oriented displacement sums including zero. For probability tables use squared Hellinger distance \(d_{\mathrm H}^2(u,v)=\frac12\sum_z(\sqrt{u_z}-\sqrt{v_z})^2\).

There is no finite absolute constant \(C\) such that

\[
\Gamma\{X\ne Y\}
\le C\left[\sqrt{2^nq-1}+\operatorname{TV}(p^{\mathrm{mid}},p)\right]
\]

for every \(n\ge1\) and every such table admitting a finite-valued globally log-concave extension \(f:\mathbb R^n\to[0,\infty)\) satisfying \(f(z)=p_z\) at every lattice point, including every zero. Here global log-concavity means \(f((1-s)x+sy)\ge f(x)^{1-s}f(y)^s\) for all real points \(x,y\) and \(0<s<1\), with a zero endpoint making the right-hand side zero.

More precisely, for each integer \(L\ge4\), put \(t=2^{-L}\), \(m_i=L2^{i-1}-1\) for \(1\le i\le L\), \(\nu=1+L(2^L-2)\), \(N=2^\nu/t=2^{\nu+L}\), and \(n_L=N\nu\). The explicit construction below gives an admissible seed \(p\) on \(\mathbb Z^\nu\) satisfying

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Gamma\{X\ne Y\}&\ge\frac{t}{2^\nu},\\
2^\nu q-1&\le\frac{9t^2}{2^\nu},\\
d_{\mathrm H}^2(p,p^{\mathrm{mid}})&\le\frac{14t^2}{2^\nu}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(P_L=p^{\otimes N}\), let \(q_L\), \(\Gamma_L\), and \(P_L^{\mathrm{mid}}\) be the corresponding quantities in dimension \(n_L\). They satisfy

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Gamma_L\{X\ne Y\}&\ge1-e^{-1},\\
0<\sqrt{2^{n_L}q_L-1}+\operatorname{TV}(P_L^{\mathrm{mid}},P_L)
&\le10\,2^{-L/2},\\
\frac{\Gamma_L\{X\ne Y\}}
{\sqrt{2^{n_L}q_L-1}+\operatorname{TV}(P_L^{\mathrm{mid}},P_L)}
&\ge\frac{2^{L/2}}{20},\\
G(P_L)&\ge\frac{2^\nu}{2\sqrt t}\longrightarrow\infty.
\end{aligned}
\]
